people.narrative: Walter Figel is the most contested witness in the American nuclear-incursion record, and he is contested in an unusual way: both sides of the Malmstrom dispute cite him, and neither has produced a statement he wrote himself. people.label: Robert J. Kaminski

people.narrative: Robert Kaminski is the one witness in the Malmstrom cluster who was close to the hardware rather than to the story, and his account is in direct and checkable tension with the Air Force's own paper. He is described as a Boeing engineer on the team sent to Malmstrom after the Echo Flight shutdown. In a 1997 letter to researcher Jim Klotz he wrote that the investigation team found nothing that would explain ten missiles dropping off alert, no significant failures and no engineering data that accounted for it, and that the inquiry was ordered ended mid-stream with no report to be filed. The first half of that is corroborated by the 341st Strategic Missile Wing history, which records in the engineering report's own words that the teams at Malmstrom were unable to determine a logical cause. The second half is contradicted by the same history, which records the investigation continuing at the contractor's facility through 1967, Boeing bench tests in its Network Resolution Area reproducing the fault signature, and three engineering change proposals submitted by Boeing as a result. Both cannot be wholly right, and the board records the tension rather than resolving it, because one of them is a document and the other is a letter thirty years after the fact.

entities.label: Strategic Air Command (SAC)
entities.sub: The USAF major command that owned every installation in this cluster; the institutional spine of the nuclear-incursion record, 1946 to 1992
entities.desc: THE MISSING SPINE. Every incident in this cluster happened inside Strategic Air Command, and until now the board had United States Air Force above and nothing between it and the bases. SAC owned Loring, Wurtsmith, Malmstrom, Minot, Grand Forks, F. E. Warren, Ellsworth and Walker; it ran the alert postures the 1975 documents invoke; and it is SAC command posts that appear as the reporting node in almost every primary record opened for this pass. The 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's Log for November 1975 reads almost entirely as a record of calls from 'SAC CP' and the 341st Strategic Air Command Post. The National Military Command Center's Loring memorandum of 29 October 1975 records that NORAD was informed of the incident by SAC and that the SAC Command Center reported back on the failure of the Army National Guard helicopter to locate the intruder, citing SAC CP OPS CONTROL 291954Z OCT 75. When Echo Flight went off alert at Malmstrom on 16 March 1967 it was SAC Headquarters that called in Ogden Air Materiel Area support for a complete engineering analysis within hours. The node exists so that a reader can see that these are not scattered base-level anomalies but a run of reports moving up one chain of command, and so that the base hubs have something to attach to.

entities.label: Malmstrom missile-field overflights, 7 to 19 November 1975
entities.sub: Thirteen days of reports from 341st SMW launch facilities, logged in the 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's Log, with F-106 intercepts attempted and radar contact lost
entities.desc: THE STRONGEST SINGLE ARTEFACT IN THE NUCLEAR STRAND, BECAUSE IT IS A WORKING LOG RATHER THAN A REPORT WRITTEN FOR ANYBODY. Between 7 and 19 November 1975 the 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's Log at Malmstrom AFB recorded a run of reports from Minuteman launch control facilities and launch facilities across the 341st Strategic Missile Wing's field: objects over M-1, L-3, Lima and L-6; an object illuminating a site driveway at the Harlowton launch control facility; K-1 watching a very bright object through 10x50 binoculars; L-1 reporting a tubular black object issuing from another object; height-finder radar picking up between two and seven objects at 10,000 to 13,000 feet; two F-106s scrambled; radar contact lost and the fighters broken off; and, from four separate points, the report that when the fighters arrived the lights went out and when the fighters departed the lights came back on. The log is even-handed in a way an advocate's document would not be: it records that surveillance could detect no track except known traffic, that an airline crew reported a meteor, and that on 12 November the controllers 'never had any joy (contact) on radar'. It ends with an entry marked, in the original, as the last entry pertaining to these incidents.

timeline.label: All ten Echo Flight missiles lose strategic alert at 0845
timeline.text: The 341st Strategic Missile Wing history: 'On 16 March 1967 at 0845, all sites in Echo (E) Flight, Malmstrom AFB, shutdown with No-Go indication of Channels 9 and 12 on Voice Reporting Signal Assemble (VRSA). All LF's in E Flight lost strategic alert nearly simultaneously. No other Wing I configuration lost strategic alert at that time.' timeline.label: The engineering investigation reports it cannot determine a cause
timeline.text: The Engineering Investigation Team's 'Report of Engineering Investigation of Echo Flight Incident, Malmstrom AFB, Mont. - 16 Mar 67', dated 23 March 1967 and classified Secret, is the document the entire Malmstrom controversy turns on. It is footnoted on almost every page of the wing history's Echo Flight section and has never been opened by this board. Through the history it states: 'The investigation teams at Malmstrom, were unable to determine a logical cause for the incident.'

timeline.label: OOAMA concludes the cause appears to be EMP or electrostatic, by elimination
timeline.text: In an interim report of 2 June 1967 to Ballistic Systems Division at Norton AFB, Ogden Air Materiel Area reported that Boeing bench tests in its Network Resolution Area had reproduced the Echo Flight fault signature in 60 per cent of twenty applications of a 30 microsecond pulse to the C-53P Logic Coupler, and concluded: 'Due to the fact that the power tests were essentially negative, it appears that the cause of the Echo Flight problem was of the EMP or electrostatic nature.' The conclusion follows from a run of negative tests rather than from reproducing the event in the field.

timeline.text: Robert Hastings convened Dwynne Arneson, Bruce Fenstermacher, Charles Halt, Robert Jamison, Patrick McDonough, Jerry Nelson and Robert Salas at the National Press Club. Six are named on his own page as having executed affidavits. For five of the seven this is their first appearance in the public record. Walter Figel declined to sign an affidavit and did not appear.
timeline.source: Robert Hastings, 'The UFOs-Nukes Connection Press Conference', https://ufohastings.com/articles/the-ufos-nukes-connection-press-conference

timeline.label: The publishing party cold-calls the second Ellsworth witness
timeline.text: Dated on air: on 26 June 2026 the producer telephoned a Michael Johnson in South Carolina, located from a viewer's Facebook tip by an unnamed recruiter, and withheld the frame, saying nothing about November-5 and nothing about a UFO. Mario Woods was then patched in and within two minutes supplied the site, the date and, after Johnson first answered 'No', the category. NO DATED PUBLIC STATEMENT BY JOHNSON ABOUT THE EVENT EXISTS BEFORE THIS CALL.
timeline.source: Jesse Michels, video rjUdn6FklAU, at 00:03:06-00:03:45, 00:05:19-00:05:46 and 00:07:29-00:07:46, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rjUdn6FklAU

timeline.label: The Ellsworth claim is published with both witnesses, and contradicts its own recording
timeline.text: Jesse Michels published video rjUdn6FklAU, 2:47:21, presenting Mario Woods and Michael Johnson on the 18 November 1977 Launch Facility November-5 claim. Its on-camera retelling of the moment of recognition at 00:17:46-00:18:11 says Johnson recognised the event with nothing supplied; its own recording of that moment at 00:07:29-00:07:46 shows an initial 'No', then Woods naming the UFO twice, then assent. Both passages are timestamped in the same episode. This is the dated artefact on which the claim rests.

gaps.text: THE SINGLE HIGHEST-VALUE MISSING DOCUMENT ON THIS BOARD. 'Report of Engineering Investigation of Echo Flight Incident, Malmstrom AFB, Mont. - 16 Mar 67', by Engineering Investigation Team, 23 March 1967, classified Secret when written. It is cited by exhibit and page number on almost every page of the 341st SMW history's Echo Flight section, so its existence, authorship, date and length are already documented. Everything either side of the Malmstrom dispute says about causation is a reading of a wing historian's summary of this report. It would settle the causation question, and it would settle whether the sentence about UFO rumours being disproven rests on anything more than a Mobile Strike Team that had been at November Flight rather than Echo Flight.
gaps.wouldClose: A FOIA request to the Air Force Historical Research Agency or to NARA for the report itself, nearly sixty years on. Also worth requesting: SAC message DM 02752 of 17 March 1967, subject 'Loss of Strategic Alert Echo Flight, Malmstrom AFB'.

gaps.text: Michael Johnson's Official Military Personnel File, his DD-214 and the Article 15 nonjudicial punishment he describes on air. Any of the three would carry a date and a unit. An Article 15 dated within months of 18 November 1977 would be the strongest available independent anchor for his presence at Ellsworth and for the claimed aftermath. It is requestable by the veteran himself. Without it, the identification of this Michael Johnson as the right Michael Johnson is settled by nothing: he asks on the recorded call whether they have the right man, and the episode itself notes it is one of the most common names in the United States.
gaps.wouldClose: The veteran's own request to the National Personnel Records Center, or the 44th Missile Security Squadron duty roster for the night of 17 to 18 November 1977 from AFHRA.

gaps.text: The complete FOIA compilation from which the 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's Log was extracted. The three pages this board has read are stamped 450, 451 and 452 and carry control number 000974 over the release line of Terrence C. James, Colonel, USAF, Director of Administration, with copies to HQ USAF/DAD and HQ USAF/JACL. AT LEAST 449 PAGES OF THAT COMPILATION HAVE NEVER BEEN SEEN BY THIS BOARD, and it is the same release stream that produced the Loring, Wurtsmith, Falconbridge and Cannon material. Obtaining it would likely multiply the Tier 1 documentary base of this whole cluster in one request.
gaps.wouldClose: Identifying the compilation by its FOIA case number and requesting it in full, or locating a complete scan. The pagination and the control number are the handles.

gaps.text: AARO Historical Record Report Volume I was NOT OPENED by the pass of 19 September 2026. media.defense.gov returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch and to curl with browser headers and an aaro.mil referer. The board's existing citation of its page 30, for interviews with five former Air Force officers who served at Malmstrom, Ellsworth, Vandenberg and Minot between 1966 and 1977, stands on an earlier pass and is not re-verified here. It matters most to l-ellsworth, which has no contemporaneous document of its own.
gaps.wouldClose: A mirror of the PDF that answers this environment, or a different route to media.defense.gov. AARO caps at Tier 2 on this board in any case, per CLAUDE.md section 2.

gaps.text: Col. Frederick Meiwald's letter to Robert Salas of 1 October 1996, in facsimile. NOT OPENED. Two flatly incompatible characterisations are in public circulation: that it elaborates and supports the Oscar Flight account, and that it records his recollection as differing from Salas's and regrets being unable to help. The board's own robert-salas node currently calls it his most important corroboration. Until it is opened, the strongest-looking support in the Oscar Flight case is a document nobody here has read.
gaps.wouldClose: Hastings's 'Witch Hunt' article, which his own page names as the place the letter is reproduced, or the facsimile from any archive.

gaps.text: James Carlson's 'American, Credulous', reported at 357 pages, and his shorter 'Echo Flights of Fantasy - Anatomy of a UFO Hoax'. NEITHER WAS OPENED. Both circulate on Scribd, which this session did not reach. His position on this board is therefore reported at one remove, from Metabunk and from The UFO Chronicles. This is the largest evidentiary gap in the case against, and CLAUDE.md section 2a requires the case against to be as well sourced as the case for.
gaps.wouldClose: Any non-Scribd copy of either work, or a direct statement by Carlson at a URL this environment can open.

gaps.text: The Walter Figel audio recordings. Robert Hastings states he tape-recorded three telephone conversations with Figel in 2008, 2009 and 2010. No URL opened by this board carries the audio or a full transcript, so every quotation attributed to Figel anywhere on this board is at one remove from the artefact. Figel is the single most contested witness in the subject and the artefact that would settle what he said has never been published in full.
gaps.wouldClose: Publication of the recordings or verbatim transcripts, or an independent interview with Figel by anyone not party to the dispute.

gaps.text: Bernard C. Nalty, 'USAF Ballistic Missile Programs 1967-1968', a Top Secret 1969 USAF official history, quoted second-hand as recording that an electronic noise pulse had shut down the flight, similar to the electromagnetic pulse generated by nuclear explosions. NOT OPENED. It is the best remaining document lead on the Malmstrom causation question after the engineering report itself, because it is an independent official account rather than a wing historian's summary.
gaps.wouldClose: A declassified copy from AFHRA, NARA or the Defense Technical Information Center mirror on archive.org, which this environment can reach.

gaps.text: A June 2025 Wall Street Journal report is said to attribute the 1967 Malmstrom shutdowns to an unannounced, classified test of site vulnerability to electromagnetic pulse. IT WAS NOT OPENED and nothing on this board rests on it. If it is real it is a materially DIFFERENT claim from the unit history's, which describes an ambient pulse of unknown origin rather than a deliberate test, and the difference matters: a deliberate unannounced test is a concealment claim, not an engineering one.
gaps.wouldClose: The article itself, with its date and byline, or the Air Force sourcing it cites.

gaps.text: The Grand Forks AFB command post event dispatch of 4 November 1975 at 0301 and the detailed incident message of 5 November 1975, in their own text. NOT OPENED. These are cited as recording that shots were possibly fired from on base toward hard alert aircraft on the SAC alert ramp, and that five shots were heard in groups of three and two, naming Captain Klawon of the 321st Security Police Squadron. THIS IS THE ONLY ALLEGATION OF WEAPONS DISCHARGE ANYWHERE IN THE 1975 SEQUENCE and it is the part of the sequence this pass established least well. Grand Forks is also not named in CINCNORAD's summary message.
gaps.wouldClose: The messages themselves from the OASD 1975 compilation, or the 321st Strategic Missile Wing unit history for the period.

gaps.text: The Mansmann letters of 1983, 1985 and 1987, in facsimile. NOT OPENED, and the dates differ between sources, with both 30 January and 10 March reported for a 1983 letter to Lee Graham. Until they are opened, the misattribution flagged in research/leads/nuclear-corrections-2026-09-19.json, that the board's malmstrom-echo-flight-1967 node assigns Big Sur letters by Maj. Florenz J. Mansmann to a 'Col. Robert Mansmann' and to the Echo Flight investigation, is flagged rather than proven.
gaps.wouldClose: The facsimiles, from the UFO research archives that publish them, or from T. Scott Crain's or Lee Graham's papers.

gaps.text: The 42nd Bombardment Wing unit history for October to December 1975, held at the Air Force Historical Research Agency, and the OSI teletype of 29 October 1975 and OSI letter of 21 April 1977 titled 'Overflight of USAF Installations by Unidentified Aircraft'. None was sought or opened. The Wurtsmith precedent makes the wing history's contents genuinely unpredictable: there, the wing historian checked his own October to December 1975 history and found no reference to the incident at all. The OSI letter's title is the more interesting of the two documents, because it is an OSI characterisation eighteen months after the fact.
gaps.wouldClose: An AFHRA request for the 42 BW history, and a FOIA request to AFOSI for the 1975 teletype and the 1977 letter by title.

gaps.text: THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL UNANSWERED SECTION 2a QUESTION IN THIS CLUSTER. Neither of the two Hastings pages opened by this board states how he located any witness. No advertisements, no unit rosters, no veterans' reunions, no referral chains, no word of mouth. Roughly a dozen proposed nodes depend on the answer, because the triage rule requires every node admitted on notability to record who found the person and by what route. The two pages also give two different totals for the number of veterans interviewed, 150 and 160.
gaps.wouldClose: A dated statement by Hastings describing his sourcing method, in a book, an interview or a page. 'UFOs and Nukes: Extraordinary Encounters at Nuclear Weapons Sites' is the obvious place to look and was not opened here.
